source_title: Offenses Relating to Unlawful Use of a Drone (new Penal Law Article 280)
citation: N.Y. Penal Law art. 280 (§§ 280.00-280.15), added by Part D of ch. of the Laws of 2026 (S.9005-B/A.10005-B, FY2027 Public Protection Budget)
effective_date: Enacted May 28, 2026; effective on the 90th day after becoming law (approx. Aug. 26, 2026)
status: Enacted, not yet effective as of research date
uas_topic: Comprehensive UAS offense statute (500-ft 'prohibited space' + 'nefarious manner' conduct)
regulated_activity: Operating a drone in a 'nefarious manner' or over/within 500 ft of a defined 'prohibited space' without prior authorization
permit_or_approval_required: No general commercial/FAA exemption identified in enacted text (only a governmental-employee duty exemption)
summary: New Penal Law Article 280 creates three new drone offenses. Sec. 280.00 defines 'drone,' 'drone operating system,' 'nefarious manner' (conduct that violates or facilitates violation of the Penal Law, is intentional/unauthorized surveillance of a prohibited space, interferes with emergency operations, facilitates criminal activity, or creates significant risk of physical injury/property damage), and 'prohibited space' (any area within 500 ft of an airport; state/federal military installation; state, local, or federal correctional facility; police station; fire department station; emergency services dispatch station; a large public gathering such as a concert, festival, or sporting event; any 'critical infrastructure' as defined in Public Officers Law § 86(5); or any school as defined in Education Law § 1125(10)). Sec. 280.05, Unlawful Use of a Drone in the Second Degree (Class A misdemeanor), is committed by operating a drone in a nefarious manner, or over prohibited space without express prior approval from someone the operator reasonably believes has authority to grant it; a governmental employee acting within official duties is exempted. Sec. 280.10, First Degree (Class E felony), applies to a repeat violation or one committed in furtherance of another crime. Sec. 280.15, Aggravated (Class D felony), applies to a repeat First Degree violation. The enacting act takes effect on the 90th day after becoming law.
practical_interpretation_aec_expert: This is a sweeping new statute with a very broad 500-ft buffer around airports, correctional facilities, critical infrastructure, schools, and large public gatherings, and — unlike Texas or Florida — the enacted text does not contain a general FAA-Part-107/commercial-operator safe harbor; the only stated exemption is for government employees acting within official duties. Treat any AEC project within 500 ft of an airport, jail/prison, police/fire station, school, or critical-infrastructure facility as requiring documented prior authorization from someone with actual or apparent authority over that site before flying, once the law takes effect (~Aug. 26, 2026).
practical_interpretation_uas_procurement: N/A — no procurement or equipment-selection implication identified
practical_interpretation_legal_counsel: Because no commercial-operator exemption is apparent in the enacted text, do not assume FAA Part 107 certification alone provides a defense in New York the way it might in Texas or Florida; build a written-authorization-collection step into standard operating procedure for any project near a listed facility type, and monitor for implementing guidance or a companion bill adding a commercial exemption before the effective date. Re-verify the exact chapter law number and final signed text (this record is based on the S.9005-B bill text as passed) before citing to a client.
verification_status: Full enacted bill text (Part D, adding Penal Law Article 280 and Executive Law § 236) read directly from the NY Senate's official bill-text page for S.9005-B, including exact statutory language, exemption structure, and effective-date clause; exact final chapter-law number was not independently cross-checked against the NY Session Laws in this pass.
notes: High-priority item: confirm the final chapter number and reconfirm no amendment altered the exemption structure between passage and the Aug. 2026 effective date.

issuing_authority: New York State Police (Superintendent); New York State Legislature
source_title: Drone Procurement Restriction — 'New York State Blue List' (new Executive Law § 236)
citation: N.Y. Executive Law § 236(5), added by Part D of ch. of the Laws of 2026 (S.9005-B/A.10005-B)
effective_date: Enacted May 28, 2026; effective on the 90th day after becoming law (approx. Aug. 26, 2026)
status: Enacted, not yet effective as of research date
regulated_party: State agencies and political subdivisions of the state (not private commercial operators)
regulated_activity: Purchasing or leasing drones or drone-mitigation technology
public_agency_only: Yes — expressly limited to the state, its agencies, and political subdivisions
commercial_operator_relevance: Low for private commercial operators; High for public-agency procurement
summary: New Executive Law § 236(5) directs the Superintendent of State Police to establish a vendor registry, the 'New York State Blue List,' of vetted and approved drone and drone-mitigation-technology vendors that comply with applicable federal requirements. Once the registry is published, the state, its agencies, and any political subdivision of the state may only buy or lease drones and drone-mitigation technology from vendors on the Blue List. Section 236 separately authorizes trained police/peace officers to use detection, tracking, and (as a last resort) kinetic or non-kinetic disabling measures against a drone posing a credible threat to prohibited spaces, subject to a 48-hour reporting requirement to the Superintendent.
practical_interpretation_aec_expert: Do not assume this restriction reaches private commercial AEC firms' own equipment purchases — it binds state agencies' and political subdivisions' own procurement, not consultants generally. If bidding on a New York state or municipal task order that specifies government-purchased or government-leased UAS equipment, confirm the equipment is Blue-List-compliant once the registry is published (expected around the Aug. 2026 effective date).
practical_interpretation_uas_procurement: Before pricing public work involving client-owned or contract-furnished UAS, request the agency's current equipment, insurance, data, and support requirements. Do not assume an internal acquisition policy governs firm-owned aircraft unless the contract incorporates it.
practical_interpretation_legal_counsel: Do not represent to a client that New York law restricts a private firm's choice of UAS manufacturer for its own equipment; confirm whether a specific public-agency contract independently incorporates Blue List compliance as a contract term (a contract-specific question) once the registry exists — it did not yet exist as of the research date.
verification_status: Full enacted bill text read directly from the NY Senate's official bill-text page for S.9005-B; the Blue List registry itself had not yet been published as of the research date, so its actual content could not be verified.
notes: Re-check whether the New York State Blue List registry has been published and what vendors/equipment appear on it once the law takes effect.

source_title: UAS Launch/Land/Operate Permit Requirement on State Park Lands
citation: 9 N.Y.C.R.R. §§ 372.7(b)-(j), 409.1(c),(j); N.Y. Parks, Recreation and Historic Preservation Law § 3.09(2)
regulated_activity: Launching, landing, or operating a UAS on OPRHP-administered land or water
requirement_type: Permit required (recreational Special UAS Permit; commercial/other activity permit)
summary: OPRHP regulations (9 NYCRR § 372.7, statewide; § 409.1, Palisades region) prohibit unauthorized launching, landing, or operation of a UAS on lands and waters it administers. Recreational UAS use requires an operator to apply for a Special UAS Permit specifying the time, place, and manner of use. Commercial UAS use is authorized under PRHPL § 3.09(2) and 9 NYCRR §§ 372.7(b)/409.1(c), which generally require a permit for any commercial activity within OPRHP facilities.
practical_interpretation_aec_expert: Treat any New York state park, historic site, or parkway the same as other permit-controlled public land for launch/land/operate purposes — apply for the applicable commercial-activity permit before staging AEC UAS work (inspection, environmental documentation, corridor mapping) on OPRHP property, and build permit lead time into scheduling.
practical_interpretation_agency_practiti: Start with the site manager or permitting office for NYS Office of Parks, Recreation and Historic Preservation (OPRHP) before scheduling fieldwork, because property-specific conditions may control the route and timing. Request the current form, lead time, fee, insurance and FAA-document checklist, and site restrictions, then keep the signed approval and conditions in the mission file.
practical_interpretation_uas_procurement: N/A — no procurement or equipment-selection implication identified
practical_interpretation_legal_counsel: Retain the OPRHP commercial-activity/UAS permit in the project file for any launch, landing, or operation on OPRHP land; confirm current permit procedure directly with the relevant OPRHP region given some variation between the statewide rule and region-specific rules (e.g., Palisades).

source_title: Prohibition on UAS Launch/Land/Operate in DEC Wilderness, Primitive, and Canoe Areas
citation: DEC Acquisition and Use of Unmanned Aircraft Policy; DEC land-classification rules for Wilderness/Primitive/Canoe areas (Adirondack/Catskill Park land classifications)
source_type: Official agency policy / binding administrative regulation
regulated_activity: Launching, landing, or operating a UAS within a DEC-classified Wilderness, Primitive, or Canoe area
requirement_type: Prohibition (in classified areas); written regional-director permission required elsewhere on DEC land
permit_or_approval_required: No (prohibition in classified areas; permission-based elsewhere)
summary: DEC prohibits launching, landing, or operating a UAS on DEC land classified as Wilderness, Primitive, or Canoe area (consistent with the general prohibition on motorized equipment in those classifications under the Adirondack/Catskill Park State Land Master Plans). On other DEC lands, written permission from the relevant regional director is generally required before UAS takeoff, landing, or operation.
practical_interpretation_aec_expert: Check the land classification of any DEC parcel near a project site before planning a launch — Wilderness/Primitive/Canoe classifications are a hard no-fly for launch/landing regardless of project purpose, while other DEC lands require regional-director permission obtained in advance.
practical_interpretation_agency_practiti: Start with the site manager or permitting office for NYS Department of Environmental Conservation (DEC) before scheduling fieldwork, because property-specific conditions may control the route and timing. Request the current form, lead time, fee, insurance and FAA-document checklist, and site restrictions, then keep the signed approval and conditions in the mission file.
practical_interpretation_uas_procurement: N/A — no procurement or equipment-selection implication identified
practical_interpretation_legal_counsel: Retain written regional-director permission in the project file for any DEC-land launch/land/operate activity outside a classified no-fly area; confirm current classification and permission procedure directly with the relevant DEC region.

source_title: Prohibition on Using Aircraft (Including Drones) to Hunt, Locate, Drive, or Take Wildlife
regulated_activity: Using a UAS to hunt, locate, drive, or take wildlife, or to harass wildlife by disturbing/harrying/worrying
summary: 6 NYCRR § 180.3 and ECL § 11-0923 prohibit using an aircraft — a category DEC treats as including drones — to hunt, locate, drive, or take wildlife. New York's broad statutory definition of 'taking' wildlife includes disturbing, harrying, or worrying it, so a drone flown too close to wildlife may separately violate this standard. A narrow, case-by-case allowance exists for recovering already-harvested game, but a drone should not be airborne while hunting is still actively underway.
practical_interpretation_aec_expert: Plan environmental-monitoring, habitat-mapping, or resource-inventory UAS flights to avoid disturbing, harrying, or worrying wildlife, and avoid any use that could be read as locating or driving game during an active hunting season.
practical_interpretation_uas_procurement: N/A — no procurement or equipment-selection implication identified
practical_interpretation_legal_counsel: Document the survey/mapping purpose of any UAS flight over wildlife habitat to distinguish it from a hunting-assistance or harassment use; the 'disturbing/harrying/worrying' standard is broad and judgment-based, so build a conservative standoff buffer into standard operating procedure near known wildlife concentrations.
verification_status: Citations and substance confirmed via a secondary industry-compliance summary; DEC's own regulations page for this rule could not be independently re-fetched (returned no content) in this pass.
notes: Recommend direct verification of 6 NYCRR § 180.3 and ECL § 11-0923 text via the NY Department of State eRules database or DEC's own site before citing to a client.

summary: New York's professional-conduct rules for licensed engineers and land surveyors require practicing and performing work only in fields in which the licensee is, by education and/or experience, fully competent and proficient. source_title: Standalone Correctional-Facility Drone Bills (S.2125/S.1380/S.2660/S.694-A and successors) — Not Independently Enacted
source_type: Proposed or pending authority (repeatedly introduced; superseded in substance by enacted Penal Law art. 280)
status: Not enacted as standalone legislation; overlapping subject matter enacted via Penal Law art. 280 (NY-001) effective ~Aug. 2026
regulated_party: Any person operating a UAS near a correctional facility
regulated_activity: Operating a UAS within a defined distance of a correctional facility
requirement_type: Proposed prohibition (various versions: 1,000 ft in earlier sessions; Governor's FY2026-27 executive budget proposed 500 ft)
summary: A standalone bill prohibiting drone operation within a set distance (1,000 ft in earlier Senate versions; the Governor's FY2026-27 executive budget proposal used 500 ft) of a state or local correctional facility, with a civil penalty for a first offense and misdemeanor exposure for subsequent offenses, has been introduced in most legislative sessions since at least 2017 (S.2125, S.1380, S.2660, S.694-A) without independently passing as a standalone act. The subject matter was ultimately addressed through the broader, independently-enacted Penal Law Article 280 (see NY-001), which includes correctional facilities within its 500-ft 'prohibited space' definition effective on the law's Aug. 2026 effective date.
practical_interpretation_aec_expert: Do not track this bill series as a separate compliance requirement — the operative correctional-facility protection for AEC purposes going forward is the enacted Penal Law Article 280 500-ft prohibited-space rule (NY-001), not this superseded bill lineage.
practical_interpretation_uas_procurement: N/A — no procurement or equipment-selection implication identified
practical_interpretation_legal_counsel: Do not represent to a client that a standalone New York correctional-facility drone statute with a 1,000-ft or 500-ft buffer exists independent of Penal Law Article 280; rely on NY-001 for current and forthcoming correctional-facility UAS restrictions in New York.
verification_status: Bill history (repeated introduction across 2017, 2019, 2021, and 2025 sessions without independent passage) confirmed via nysenate.gov bill listings and a secondary news source describing a 2017 Senate passage that did not complete the legislative process; superseding effect of Penal Law art. 280 inferred from that statute's 'prohibited space' definition, which independently covers correctional facilities.
